forces: Voice (alto), alto flute, viola, guitar, vibraphone, xylorimba and percussion
performers: Marie-Thérèse Cahn, voice; J. Tiberge, flute; Collot, viola; A. Stingl, guitar; J. Delecluse, vibraphone; P. Naudin, xylorimba; A. Cavaille, percussion; Pierre Boulez, conductor
intro: The second side of Boulez’s Vega recording of Le Marteau sans maître holds movements VI to IX: the sung “Bourreaux de solitude”, two instrumental pieces, and the closing “Bel édifice et les pressentiments”, for which the whole ensemble plays.

cues.title: Movement VI: “Bourreaux de solitude”
cues.text: The sung setting of Char’s “Bourreaux de solitude”, the poem that the earlier Commentaires comment on. Lonchampt calls it the most austere piece of the work, and hears complementary rhythms among the instruments at the start, perhaps inherited from Webern’s Symphony, Op. 21.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on Bourreaux de solitude. Commentaires as purely instrumental pieces and the poems set: Souvtchinsky’s note on the Vega C 35 A 67 sleeve (note by Pierre Souvtchinsky, credits), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/c-35-a-67-boulez-o-le-marteau-sans-maitre-pierre-boulez
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The companion disc, C 30 A 66
cues.text: Vega’s companion disc C 30 A 66, headed as the fourth concert of 1956, holds extracts of Le Marteau with Webern’s Symphony and Lieder, Nono’s Incontri and Stockhausen’s Kontra-Punkte, all conducted by Boulez.
cues.evidence: Track list of the Vega disc “Les Concerts du Domaine Musical – IVe Concert 1956”, Internet Archive item lp_les-concerts-du-domaine-musical-ive-conc_anton-webern-luigi-nono-karlheinz-stockhau: https://archive.org/details/lp_les-concerts-du-domaine-musical-ive-conc_anton-webern-luigi-nono-karlheinz-stockhau . Catalogue number and conductor: L’Express, 12 November 1959, “Quelques disques de musique contemporaine”: https://archive.org/details/sim_express_1959-11-12_439

cues.title: Movement VII: three instruments
cues.text: Après “L’Artisanat furieux” is the shortest movement. Lonchampt finds it close to the first movement, written for three instruments, with a rhythmic play that is easy to follow.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on Après L’Artisanat furieux.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Movement VIII: Commentaire III
cues.text: Commentaire III resembles Commentaire I: Lonchampt hears the flute solo and the harsh double notes of the xylorimba laid over one another. The percussion has a formal role, playing claves, then a double bell, then bongos.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on Commentaire III.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Grand Prix du Disque
cues.text: L’Express listed this disc on 12 November 1959 as the complete version of the work, conducted by Boulez with M. T. Cahn, and noted that it had won the Grand Prix du Disque of the Académie Charles-Cros.
cues.evidence: L’Express, 12 November 1959, “Quelques disques de musique contemporaine”: https://archive.org/details/sim_express_1959-11-12_439 (“Version intégrale … Grand Prix du Disque ; Académie Charles-Cros. Vega C 35 A 67”).

cues.title: Boulez and René Char
cues.text: The three poems come from René Char’s collection Le Marteau sans maître. Boulez had already set Char in Le Visage nuptial, composed in 1946.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981 (the poems and Visage nuptial of 1946). First version of Visage nuptial, October 1946: Philharmonie de Paris and French Ministry of Culture, Pierre Boulez archival biography, https://www.pierreboulez.org/default/biographie.aspx?_lg=en-US

cues.title: Movement IX: the whole ensemble
cues.text: In the second “Bel édifice et les pressentiments” the whole ensemble plays together for the only time in the work. Lonchampt hears a free, recitative-like tempo at the start and quotations from earlier movements.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on the last piece: “réunie au complet pour la seule dernière pièce”; “tempo libre de récit”; “citations des pièces antérieures”.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Voice and flute without words
cues.text: The voice is soon freed from the text and uses Sprechgesang at moments. It then alternates wordless phrases with the flute, supported by the ensemble except for the percussion.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on Bel édifice et les pressentiments (version 2).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute and deep percussion
cues.text: The movement closes with the flute against two low tam-tams and a gong. Lonchampt describes the mood as recollected (“recueillie”).
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981: the flute, “précisément accompagnée par les percussions profondes (deux tam-tams graves et gong)”, concludes “dans une ambiance recueillie”.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marie-Thérèse Cahn (voice (alto)), J. Tiberge (flute), Collot (viola), A. Stingl (guitar), J. Delecluse (vibraphone), P. Naudin (xylorimba), A. Cavaille (percussion), Pierre Boulez (conductor)
fields.note: Names as printed on the Vega sleeve, where each instrumentalist is preceded by “M.” (Monsieur) and not all have a first name. The Internet Archive description reads “Stingj” and “Cabaille”, which are misreadings of “Stingl” and “Cavaille” on the sleeve. The archival biography names Marie-Thérèse Cahn as the mezzo-soprano of the Domaine musical performance of 21 March 1956.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Nine-movement version as performed in the 1956 season, before Boulez’s revision of 1957; second of two files, holding movements VI–IX.
fields.note: The sleeve lists nine movements in the final order. The Wikipedia article and the archival biography place Boulez’s further revision, and the engraved Universal Edition score (UE 12450), in 1957, after this recording. MusicWeb’s review of the Accord reissue labels a 1956 recording by Cahn and Boulez, 30 min 44 s long, as the “1955 version”. The sleeve does not name an edition.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 1956, season of the Domaine musical (fourth concert)
fields.note: The sleeve reads “Les Concerts du Domaine musical, 4me concert – saison 1956”, and Boulez’s 1963 discography reads “Enregistrement saison 1956”. Neither gives a day, and neither says whether the disc was made at a concert or in a studio session. The archival biography dates the French première, the first Domaine musical concert Boulez conducted in full, to 21 March 1956; the sources do not say that this is the fourth concert of the sleeve. A Discogs entry for the LP carries a contributor’s note “Recorded live in 1956” and names the Petit Théâtre Marigny as the place; the sleeve says neither, and the silences between the movements in this file contain only low-level noise.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue or studio is named on the sleeve. The Domaine musical gave its concerts at the Petit Marigny in 1956, but that does not establish where the disc was recorded.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Vega, 25 cm 33⅓ rpm LP, series “Présence de la musique contemporaine”
fields.note: The item description reads “C 35 A 67, disque microsillon 25 cm Véga”. The sleeve adds that the recording was made “sous les auspices du Conseil International de la Musique avec le concours de l’UNESCO”.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: L’Express of 12 November 1959 and Boulez’s 1963 discography both give C 35 A 67 as the “version intégrale”. The extracts disc, Vega C 30 A 66, is a different issue.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 2 (file f2, labelled “fin”): movements VI–IX; side 1 (file f1): movements I–V
fields.note: The item description lists f1 as “Le Marteau sans maître” and f2 as “Le Marteau sans maître (fin)” and does not list movements per side; Discogs lists A1–A5 as movements I–V and B1–B4 as VI–IX. In this file the music begins after about one second of digital silence and three silences of about 4 to 7 seconds end at 3:12, 4:13 and 9:59; the sound ends at about 16:57. They divide the side into four pieces of about 3:07, 0:56, 5:40 and 6:58, which agree with the lengths of movements VI–IX in the 1956 recording as listed by MusicBrainz for a later reissue (3:09, 1:01, 5:41, 6:58; 16 min 49 s in all). The side begins with “Bourreaux de solitude”, the movement after the one that ends side 1. Matrix numbers are not shown.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item is in the Internet Archive’s Hifidelity collection. Its description ends with a shelf mark (“Localisation: Af-10”), which suggests a library catalogue entry; no transfer engineer or institution is named. The uploader’s account is an email address, which is not reproduced.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item became public on 2 July 2021; that is an upload date, not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The item offers FLAC, WAV and MP3 files for each side. Equalisation, noise reduction and speed correction are not described. The MP3 has about one second of digital silence at the start and about three at the end.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Boulez died in 2016, so the work is in copyright in the EU, under the life-plus-70 term, until the end of 2086.
fields.note: Boulez’s death on 5 January 2016 is recorded in the archival biography; the term is our calculation. The poems are by René Char (1907–1988) and are also in copyright. Rights in the composition and in the poems are separate from rights in the recording. No United States status is claimed.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: first published in 1956 (before 1963); US status not established.
fields.note: The archival biography lists the Véga record release of the work under 1956; L’Express lists the disc on 12 November 1959; Boulez’s 1963 book lists it. A French phonogram published in 1956 had run its 50-year term by the end of 2006 and was not revived by the 2011 extension, which applies to fixations still protected on 1 November 2013. No United States clearance is claimed. The Internet Archive item carries no licence and no litigation or restriction marker. The sleeve does not say whether the recording was made at a concert; a Discogs contributor’s note says it was recorded live. The basis here is publication of the commercial Vega LP, which L’Express documents by November 1959.

composer.epithet: Composer of music built on explosive attacks and long echoes, who also founded the ensembles, concert series and laboratories needed to perform it.
facts: Messiaen: harmony · Andrée Vaurabourg: counterpoint · René Leibowitz: twelve-note composition
Joined the Renaud–Barrault company in 1946, playing the ondes Martenot
BBC Symphony Orchestra, 1971–75 · New York Philharmonic, 1971–77
Domaine musical, 1954 · Ensemble intercontemporain, 1976 · IRCAM opened in 1977
composer.background:
Pierre Boulez arrived in Paris in 1943 after studying advanced mathematics in Lyon and turning down the engineering career his father wanted for him. He was eighteen and came from Montbrison in central France. Within two years he had won a first prize in harmony at the Conservatoire. His teacher, Olivier Messiaen, also held private classes in which students analysed Debussy’s Jeux and Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring.

Messiaen’s classroom required concentration. Horn and piano classes could be heard nearby while the students took musical dictation. ‘You learned to listen without sound’, Boulez recalled to Jed Distler in a London interview in August 2000, explaining why he never composed at the piano. He took counterpoint lessons with Andrée Vaurabourg and studied twelve-note music with René Leibowitz, who introduced him to the music of Schoenberg and Webern. By 1946 Boulez had broken with Leibowitz, impatient with his reverence for Schoenberg’s methods.
